title: The Sin Offering: When Israel Goes Wrong Without Meaning To
summary: The LORD gives the law of the sin offering for anyone who breaks one of his commands unintentionally. The chapter works down the ranks of Israel: the anointed priest and the whole congregation each bring a bull whose blood is carried into the Tent of Meeting, a leader brings a male goat, and an ordinary Israelite brings a female goat or lamb. Each time the priest makes atonement, and in each of the last three cases the text adds that the offender will be forgiven.
story: Chapters 1 to 3 described offerings a worshiper brought freely, gifts of devotion and celebration. Chapter 4 opens a new speech from the LORD and a new subject: what happens when Israel fails. The tabernacle is God's house in the middle of the camp, and the question that drives Leviticus is how he can stay there among people who keep going wrong. The answer starts here, with the most ordinary kind of failure, the wrong done without planning it and often without noticing it at first. The offering introduced in this chapter will return again and again: at the ordination of the priests (chapter 8), in the rites that close a woman's recovery from childbirth and a person's recovery from skin disease (chapters 12 and 14), and above all on the Day of Atonement (chapter 16), when its blood is carried into the Most Holy Place itself. Chapter 5 continues the same offering with specific cases and a sliding scale for the poor.
historical:
Chapter 4 sketches the structure of Israel's community in the wilderness camp. At the top stands the anointed priest, Aaron and his successors, the figure later called the high priest. Then comes the whole congregation, represented by its elders, who lay their hands on the bull (verse 15). The leader of verse 22 translates nasi, the word Numbers uses for the heads of the tribes (Numbers 1:16; 7:2); Ezekiel later uses it for the prince of a restored Israel, who provides a bull as a sin offering for himself and the people (Ezekiel 45:22). Last come the common people, literally the people of the land, meaning ordinary members of the community. The law assumes that anyone on this ladder can go wrong, and that rank raises the stakes. When the anointed priest sins, he brings guilt on the people (verse 3).

Israel's neighbors worried about unknown offenses too. Mesopotamian penitential prayers have a sufferer plead with any god he may have angered, confessing sins he cannot name in the hope of finding the deity behind his troubles. Leviticus 4 belongs to a different world. There is one God, his commands are known, and when the offender becomes aware of the sin, a remedy is already in place, followed by a promise: he will be forgiven.
cultural:
The chapter assumes the layout of the tabernacle. Outside, in the courtyard, stood the bronze altar of burnt offering. Inside the tent was the Holy Place, with the golden altar of incense, the lampstand, and the table, and beyond a veil lay the Most Holy Place with the ark. Where the blood goes depends on who sinned. For a leader or a commoner the priest daubs blood on the horns of the courtyard altar. For the anointed priest or the whole congregation he carries it inside, sprinkles it seven times before the veil, and puts it on the horns of the incense altar. The horns were projections at the altar's four corners, the most sacred part of it; a fugitive could grab them to claim sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50), and a large horned altar built of cut stones has been found at Beersheba.

Many scholars, following Jacob Milgrom, argue that sin and impurity were thought to pollute God's sanctuary itself, reaching deeper into it the graver the offense, and that the sin offering's blood purged that pollution so God could keep living among his people. Others, such as Roy Gane, argue that the ordinary sin offering cleansed the offender, with the sanctuary purged once a year on the Day of Atonement. Both agree that sin is not a private matter here; it touches the place where God dwells. When blood had been carried inside, the carcass could not be eaten and was burned outside the camp at the clean place where the altar's ashes were dumped (verses 11-12).
literary: The chapter is case law arranged by rank, from the top of Israel's society to the bottom: the anointed priest (verses 3-12), the whole congregation (13-21), a leader (22-26), and one of the common people (27-35), who may bring either a goat or a lamb. The first two cases are long and nearly identical, and the offering is the same costly bull, since priest and people together carry the community's standing before God. The later cases shrink in cost and ritual, but not in result. A refrain closes each of the last three cases: the priest will make atonement, and he or they will be forgiven (verses 20, 26, 31, 35). The anointed priest's case lacks the forgiveness line, and interpreters have offered reasons without agreeing on one. Small cross-references show a manual building on itself, as when the fat is removed just as from the peace offering (verses 10, 26, 31, 35). An old rabbinic comment noticed that the leader's case alone begins with the Hebrew word asher, when, and heard in it a pun on ashrei, happy: happy the people whose leader admits his failures.

outline.t: When one of the common people sins

doctrines.note: Sin here is real even when it is unintended. The offender incurs guilt before he knows it and must act once he becomes aware. The chapter treats sin as a breach of God's commands with consequences for the community and the sanctuary, not merely a bad intention.
Atonement is God's provision, not a human bargain. The animal dies, its blood is applied where God dwells, and the priest mediates. The result is stated as a promise from God: they will be forgiven.

Leaders are held to account first and most expensively. The anointed priest's sin affects everyone, and his offering matches the whole congregation's. Holiness in Israel was never a private achievement; it was the health of a community living around God's house.

words.note: Chattat, sin offering. The same Hebrew word means sin, and a related verb means to purify. Because the offering is also required after childbirth and recovery from skin disease, where no moral wrong is involved, many scholars prefer to call it the purification offering. The traditional name is not wrong, but the offering deals with the effects of both sin and impurity.

Kipper, to make atonement. Its origin is debated. Some connect it with covering, others with wiping clean or purging, and others with the related noun kopher, a ransom paid for a life (Exodus 30:12). In Leviticus it is usually the priest who performs it, most often by means of blood, and the result is a restored relationship between God and his people.

Salach, to forgive. In the Hebrew Bible this verb only ever has God as its subject. People can pardon one another in other words, but this forgiveness belongs to God alone. That is why the chapter's refrain matters: the priest acts, but it is God who forgives.

christ: The New Testament draws directly on this chapter. Hebrews 13:11-12 points to the sin offering whose blood was carried into the sanctuary while its body was burned outside the camp: “And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.” Paul writes that God sent his Son “as an offering for sin” (Romans 8:3), using the Greek phrase the ancient Greek translation of Leviticus uses for this very offering. Some interpreters read 2 Corinthians 5:21, where God “made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,” in the same light, though others take it more generally. Leviticus 4 also sets up a problem that the New Testament answers. The priest who offers for others is himself a sinner who needs a bull for his own guilt. Hebrews presents Jesus as a high priest who needs no offering for himself and who offers his own blood once for all.

hard.q: If the sin offering only covers unintentional sins, what happens to people who sin on purpose?
hard.a:
Leviticus 4 limits itself to unintentional wrongs, and Numbers 15:30-31 says that the person who sins defiantly is cut off, with his guilt remaining on him. Read alone, that looks as though deliberate sin had no remedy. The rest of the law is more complex. Leviticus 6:1-7 provides a guilt offering for someone who has lied under oath and cheated a neighbor, which is plainly deliberate, once he confesses and makes restitution. The Day of Atonement cleanses Israel from all its sins, including its rebellious acts (16:16, 21). David, guilty of adultery and murder, found no offering prescribed for his crimes, yet he prayed, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

Many interpreters therefore distinguish the defiant sin of Numbers 15, done by someone who despises God's word and refuses to repent, from deliberate sins that are later confessed. A later rabbinic saying holds that repentance turns deliberate sins into errors. Christians have read the New Testament's offer of forgiveness in the same way, as open to anyone who turns back to God, whatever the sin.

questions: The chapter assumes people can sin without knowing it. What might you be doing wrong right now that you have not yet noticed, and how would you find out?
The anointed priest's offering cost as much as the whole congregation's. What does that say about how leaders in a church or family should treat their own failures?
Forgiveness in this chapter follows a public act at God's house. Why might it matter that confession and forgiveness are not only private and inward?
